Exact kriging cross-validation from a covariance matrix

Source: R/engine.R
kcv_engine.Rd

Low-level engine behind kcv(), implemented in C++. Given the covariance matrix C of the observations, the trend matrix F and fold assignments, it computes cross-validation predictions and variances for every fold from a single factorization of C:

Usage

kcv_engine(C, F, y, folds, beta = NULL)

kcv_engine_prepare(C, F, beta = NULL)

kcv_engine_run(prepared, y, folds, beta = NULL)

Arguments

C

n x n covariance matrix of the observations (symmetric positive definite; an asymmetric matrix or a non-finite entry is an error).

F

n x p trend matrix (a column of ones for ordinary kriging).

y

Response: a numeric vector or an n x T matrix. Each column is cross-validated with the same kriging weights.

folds

Vector of length n of fold identifiers.

beta

Optional trend coefficients for simple kriging: a length-p vector shared by every column of y, or a p x T matrix with one column per column of y. In kcv_engine_run(), replaces the coefficients given to kcv_engine_prepare(), which must have been made with beta (the factorization of simple kriging does not depend on beta).

prepared

A kcv_prepared object from kcv_engine_prepare() or kcv_prepare().

Value

kcv_engine() and kcv_engine_run() return a list with pred (n x T matrix), var (length-n vector; the same for every column of y) and folds. kcv_engine_prepare() returns a kcv_prepared object holding the factorization, to be passed to kcv_engine_run() any number of times with different y or folds.

Details

  • ordinary/universal kriging (beta = NULL, trend re-estimated by GLS in each fold): \(Q = C^{-1} - C^{-1}F(F'C^{-1}F)^{-1}F'C^{-1}\);

  • simple kriging (known beta): \(Q = C^{-1}\), applied to \(y - F\beta\).

For a fold \(I\), the residual is \(e_I = Q_{II}^{-1}(Qy)_I\), the prediction \(y_I - e_I\), and the prediction-error variance \(\mathrm{diag}(Q_{II}^{-1})\).

Only the diagonal blocks \(Q_{II}\) are formed, never the full \(n \times n\) matrix \(Q\). Leave-one-out (every fold of size one) uses \(e_i = (Qy)_i / Q_{ii}\) and \(1 / Q_{ii}\) directly.

Memory

Factorizing C needs one \(n \times n\) workspace in addition to C, so the peak memory of kcv_engine() is about \(16 n^2\) bytes. (The model-based kcv() builds the covariance directly in the workspace and needs half of that.) Because operating systems often over-commit memory, an allocation that is too large may not fail cleanly, so the estimate is checked up front against a budget of getOption("fastkcv.max_gb", 6.4) GB, which allows \(n\) up to about 20,000 here and 28,000 in kcv(). Raise it with options(fastkcv.max_gb = ) on machines with enough memory. A prepared object keeps its \(n \times n\) factor (\(8 n^2\) bytes) for as long as it exists.

See also

kcv_prepare() and kcv_run() for the model-based equivalent.

Examples

set.seed(1)
xy <- matrix(runif(100), ncol = 2)
C <- exp(-as.matrix(dist(xy)) / 0.3)
y <- rnorm(50)
res <- kcv_engine(C, matrix(1, 50, 1), y, folds = seq_len(50))
head(res$pred)
#>             [,1]
#> [1,] -1.25265287
#> [2,]  0.29321589
#> [3,]  0.43726382
#> [4,]  0.01225811
#> [5,] -0.04605711
#> [6,] -0.27491546

# Factorize once, then cross-validate several fold schemes.
p <- kcv_engine_prepare(C, matrix(1, 50, 1))
loo <- kcv_engine_run(p, y, seq_len(50))
k5 <- kcv_engine_run(p, y, rep(1:5, 10))
